name: Hellaby's Kruskal Universe of Dust
description: A spherically symmetric universe of inhomogeneous dust with two regions joined by a dynamical neck.
convention: We use units with $G=c=1$ and take the Ricci tensor as $R_{\mu\nu}=R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: A neck joins two regions of a universe filled with dust [hellaby1987]. The neck opens at a white hole and closes at a black hole, with a big bang in its past and a big crunch in its future [hellaby1987]. Charles Hellaby described such a spacetime in 1987, with the same two sheet topology as the extended Schwarzschild solution and a nonzero density [hellaby1987].¶Each shell of dust keeps its radial coordinate $r$ as its areal radius $Y(t,r)$ changes with time $t$. In units with $G=c=1$, the spherical line element is $ds^2=-dt^2+Y'^2dr^2/(1+f)+Y^2d\Omega^2$, where a prime means a derivative with respect to $r$ and $f(r)$ is twice the energy per unit mass of a shell [hellaby2002]. The radius obeys $\dot Y^2=2M/Y+f$, with $M(r)$ the gravitational mass function and a dot denoting a derivative with respect to $t$ [hellaby2002]. The density $\rho$ obeys $8\pi\rho=2M'/(Y^2Y')$ away from the neck [hellaby2002].¶Hellaby and Andrzej Krasiński chose $M=M_0(1+M_1r^2)^3$, $f=-e^{-r^2/r_s}$, and $a=-\pi M/(-f)^{3/2}$ for a symmetric dust wormhole, where $M_0$, $M_1$, and $r_s$ are positive constants and $a(r)$ is the time of the bang [hellaby2002]. At $r=0$, the function $f$ reaches $-1$ and the areal radius reaches a minimum on a spatial slice. Both $Y'$ and $1+f$ vanish at the neck, and the radial metric component has a finite limit there [hellaby2002].¶Every shell in this example expands and then contracts, and the moment of maximum expansion is $t=0$ [hellaby2002]. The apparent horizons meet at the neck at that moment, where $Y=2M$ [hellaby2002]. A light ray can cross the neck, but a ray that enters the trapped region cannot emerge past the apparent horizon on the other side [hellaby2002].¶When $M_1=0$, the dust density vanishes and the Schwarzschild geometry remains [hellaby2002]. Like the Schwarzschild geometry, the dust model is spherically symmetric, and its mass function increases away from the neck on each side [hellaby2002]. Hellaby and Krasiński extended the discussion to the Szekeres dust models, whose shells need not be concentric [hellaby2002].

related.text: Dust whose density and energy vary from shell to shell. Its energy function $E$ obeys $1+2E=0$ at the neck, where $f=2E$ [hellaby2002].
The vacuum member of the same construction, with the mass constant from shell to shell [hellaby2002].
Two sheets of Schwarzschild space joined at a smallest sphere, with a black hole and a white hole in the extended geometry [einstein1935, kruskal1960].
A uniform ball of dust collapsing inside Schwarzschild's vacuum [oppenheimersnyder1939].
Dust whose spherical shells need not be concentric, with a neck that joins two regions [hellaby2002].
A portion of a closed universe of dust joined to Schwarzschild's exterior behind a throat [hsu2008unitarity].
Spherical dust on a tube of spheres that share one radius at each time [ruban1968, krasinski1999datt].

coordinates.name: Comoving Synchronous

parameters.description: Areal radius, a length, determined by $Y=M(1-\cos\eta)/(-f)$ and $t=a+M(\eta-\sin\eta)/(-f)^{3/2}$, with $0<\eta<2\pi$.
Twice the energy per unit mass of a shell, $f=-e^{-r^2/r_s}$.
Positive radial parameter with dimensions of length squared.
Dimensionless parameter of the elliptic evolution.

coordinates.convention: We use comoving coordinates $(t,r,\theta,\phi)$, with $t$ and $r$ lengths and the two angles on each shell. At $r=0$ the radial metric component is the finite limit $g_{rr}=r_s(\partial_r^2Y)^2$ evaluated at the neck. A prime denotes a derivative with respect to $r$. In the geodesic equations a dot on a coordinate is its derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
